VIDEO.title: Matthew 11:20-30 – Why the Smartest People Miss God
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

hand: Come to Me, all who are weary and heavy-laden.
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 11:20-30. Jesus denounces Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum, the towns that saw most of His miracles and did not repent. Then He praises the Father for hiding these things from the wise and revealing them to infants, says that all things have been handed over to Him, and invites the weary to take His yoke and find rest.

The 'woes' are not vengeful. The video follows Leon Morris: Jesus is expressing regret that combines warning and compassion, so 'alas' captures the sentiment. Tyre, Sidon and Sodom stood for Israel's old enemies and for pagan wickedness, yet Jesus says they would have repented. In His eyes, miracles are invitations to repentance.

Verses 21-24 also teach degrees of judgment: it will be 'more tolerable' for Sodom than for the towns that saw the light of Christ (compare John 19:11). And they hold together God's sovereignty and human responsibility without trying to resolve the tension.

The woes echo the prophets' woes on Jerusalem (Isaiah 3:1-11; Jeremiah 13:27; Ezekiel 24:6-9). 'All things have been handed over to Me' recalls the Son of Man in Daniel 7:14 and points ahead to Matthew 28:18.

A yoke, the video says, is an idiom for a rabbi's teaching and way of life. Jesus' yoke is chrēstos, 'easy': kind and pleasant, not harsh. His rest echoes Jeremiah 6:16, where rest for the soul comes from walking in the good way.
The lesson for the original audience: God hides His activity from those who do not trust Him, and He reveals it to those who remain dependent on Him, like little children who love to be taught.
QUOTES: In the eyes of Jesus, miracles are invitations to repentance.
God hides his activity from those who do not trust him and he reveals his activity to those who remain dependent on him.
Slow down, chew on these nuggets, pause the video if necessary.
They trusted their own understanding of what God's word actually teaches.

method.p: The teacher's tip for a dense passage: slow down, chew on the nuggets, and pause if you need to. Then follow each Old Testament echo (Isaiah 3, Jeremiah 6, Daniel 7) back to its passage and read it in full.

LSB_QUOTES.text: I praise You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that You have hidden these things from the wise and intelligent and have revealed them to infants.
Come to Me, all who are weary and heavy-laden, and I will give you rest.
Stand by the ways and see and ask for the ancient paths, / Where the good way is, and walk in it; / And you will find rest for your souls.

src.text: Then He began to denounce the cities in which most of His miracles were done, because they did not repent. “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the miracles had occurred in Tyre and Sidon which occurred in you, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. Nevertheless I say to you, it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon in the day of judgment than for you.

lines.text: These are the towns where Jesus did most of His miracles, and they did not repent. Following Leon Morris, the video hears regret in 'woe': a warning mixed with compassion. 'Alas' captures it.
Tyre and Sidon stand for Israel's old enemies, yet Jesus says they would have repented in sackcloth and ashes. In His eyes, miracles are invitations to repentance.
Luke places the same woes in Jesus' instructions to the seventy (Luke 10:13-15).

src.text: And Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You will descend to Hades; for if the miracles had occurred in Sodom which occurred in you, it would have remained to this day. Nevertheless I say to you that it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom in the day of judgment, than for you.”

lines.text: Capernaum was Jesus' own base. Sodom stands for the pagan wickedness of the Canaanites, and still it would have remained.

Degrees of punishment: there is a worse judgment for towns that received the light of Christ than for pagan cities that did not. Jesus does not explain how it works, but the words are there (compare John 19:11).
Jesus' words on Capernaum echo the taunt over the king of Babylon: 'you will be brought down to Sheol' (Isaiah 14:13-15).

left.text: Woe to the wicked! It will go badly with him, / For what he has dealt out will be done to him.

right.text: ‘Therefore, thus says Lord Yahweh, / “Woe to the city of blood, / To the pot in which there is rust / And whose rust has not gone out of it! / Take out of it piece after piece, / Without making a choice.

lines.text: Jesus' woes are thematically tied to the prophets' woes on Jerusalem and Judah (Isaiah 3:1-11; Jeremiah 13:27; Ezekiel 24:6-9). Go read those passages.
Isaiah 3:5 describes people turning on one another, which recalls Jesus' warning of divided families in Matthew 10.
The passage holds together God's sovereignty and human responsibility. Jesus threatens judgment on those who chose not to repent, and then thanks the Father for hiding these things from the wise.
The Bible often places these two side by side without trying to resolve the tension, and so does this passage.
Compare Paul in Philippians 2:12-13: 'work out your salvation… for it is God who is at work in you.'

src.text: At that time Jesus said, “I praise You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that You have hidden these things from the wise and intelligent and have revealed them to infants. Yes, Father, for this way was well-pleasing in Your sight.

lines.text: The 'wise and intelligent' trusted their own conclusions about what the Messiah would do and their own reading of God's word. That blinded them to what God was doing in front of them.
Little children are humble; as D. A. Carson notes, they are dependent and they love to be taught.
Jesus says the same in 18:3-4: 'unless you are converted and become like children.'

left.text: And to Him was given dominion, / Glory, and a kingdom, / That all the peoples, nations, and men of every tongue / Might serve Him. / His dominion is an everlasting dominion / Which will not be taken away; / And His kingdom is one / Which will not be destroyed.

right.text: And Jesus came up and spoke to them, saying, “All authority has been given to Me in heaven and on earth.

lines.text: 'All things have been handed over to Me by My Father' (11:27) recalls the one like a Son of Man who comes to the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7, and foreshadows the Great Commission in Matthew 28:18.
Jesus also announces His special relationship with the Father: only the Son knows the Father, and those to whom the Son wills to reveal Him.

HIDDEN.title: Hidden from those who do not trust

lines.text: The issue was rebellion and disobedience, so the cure is humility. God hides His activity from those who do not trust Him, and He reveals it to those who remain dependent on Him.
This is where spiritual discernment begins: trusting God instead of our own conclusions.
Paul: 'God has chosen the foolish things of the world to shame the wise' (1 Corinthians 1:27).

src.text: “Come to Me, all who are weary and heavy-laden, and I will give you rest. Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For My yoke is easy and My burden is light.”

lines.text: A yoke, the video says, is a Hebrew idiom for a rabbi's teaching. A disciple wanted to be like his rabbi in every way, and that meant total obedience and dedication to his teaching and way of life.
Contrast the leaders who 'tie up heavy burdens and lay them on men's shoulders' (23:4).

src.text: Thus says Yahweh, / “Stand by the ways and see and ask for the ancient paths, / Where the good way is, and walk in it; / And you will find rest for your souls. / But they said, ‘We will not walk in it.’

lines.text: Jesus' rest is tied to Jeremiah 6:16: rest comes from walking the good path, living by the right teaching. That is why He speaks of His yoke.
Jeremiah's hearers answered, 'We will not walk in it.' The towns of 11:20-24 answered the same way.
'Easy' is chrēstos: kind, pleasant, not harsh or stern or severe. The captions spell it 'crestos.' Jesus' teaching is not a crushing load.
'Gentle' in 11:29 is praus, the same word as 'lowly' in the Beatitudes (5:5).
A later rabbinic saying speaks of 'the yoke of the Torah' (Mishnah Avot 3:5).

TERMS.def: Greek ouai, a cry of grief or warning; the video prefers 'alas.'
Rough goat-hair cloth and ashes, the signs of mourning and repentance (Jonah 3:5-6).
The realm of the dead (Hebrew Sheol); here the opposite of being 'exalted to heaven.'
The final judgment, when it will be 'more tolerable' for some than for others.
The idea that judgment is weighed by the light received (11:22-24; John 19:11; Luke 12:47-48).
Having to do with the last things and the coming judgment; the captions spell it 'esqueological.'
A wooden bar that joins animals for work; in the video, an idiom for a rabbi's teaching and way of life.
Jesus' favorite title for Himself, drawn from Daniel 7:13-14.

WORDS.gloss: Woe, alas: a cry of pain or of warning. Look up: BDAG, οὐαί.
To repent, change one's mind and way.
Hades, the realm of the dead.
Infant, little child; also the immature or simple.
Kind, good, pleasant; of a yoke, easy to wear. Look up: BDAG, χρηστός.
Woe! A cry of grief or threat. Look up: BDB or HALOT, אוֹי.

BACKGROUND.p: Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum sit within a few miles of each other on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee, where Jesus did most of His work. Today they are ruins; Chorazin's black basalt synagogue dates from centuries later.
Phoenician port cities on the coast north-west of Galilee. The prophets pronounced judgment on their pride and wealth (Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26-28); Jesus later visited their region (15:21).
Mourners and penitents wore rough goat-hair cloth and sat in or sprinkled themselves with ashes, as Nineveh did when Jonah preached (Jonah 3:5-6).

Later rabbinic sayings use the same picture: 'whoever takes upon himself the yoke of the Torah, they remove from him the yoke of government and the yoke of worldly concerns' (Mishnah Avot 3:5). Reciting the Shema is to 'accept upon himself the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven' (Mishnah Berakhot 2:2). The Mishnah was compiled about AD 200.

WITNESSES.text: And not even at this does He stay His speech, but makes their fears yet more intense… so as by every means to gather them in, both by bewailing, and by alarming them.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 37, on 11:21-24. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain).

WITNESSES.text: Wherefore neither did He say, you have revealed it to fools, but to babes; to unsophisticated, that is, to simple-minded men

WITNESSES.text: Thus He both spoke of a yoke, and called it easy; both named a burden, and added that it was light; that you should neither flee from them as toilsome, nor despise them as over easy.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 38, on 11:30. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

DEBATES.p: The video takes 'more tolerable' at face value: judgment is weighed by the light received. Most commentators agree (compare Luke 12:47-48); others read the comparison as rhetorical emphasis on Israel's guilt.
The Father hides and reveals (11:25-27), yet the towns are blamed for not repenting (11:20). The video lets both stand, as Scripture does; traditions differ on how to explain them together.
The video: a rabbi's teaching. Others see a wider picture of submission, as in the 'yoke' of a king or of wisdom (compare Sirach 51:26). Either way, Jesus offers Himself, not a heavier law.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The quotes attributed to Leon Morris ('regret, which combines warning and compassion') and D. A. Carson ('dependent and… love to be taught') are summaries we could not check against the books.
Tyre and Sidon were not always enemies: Hiram of Tyre helped David and Solomon build (1 Kings 5:1-12). The prophets' oracles against them (Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26-28) are what the video has in mind.

'Yoke' as an idiom for a rabbi's teaching rests mostly on later rabbinic sayings ('the yoke of the Torah,' Mishnah Avot 3:5, compiled about AD 200); it is a fair background, not a first-century definition.
Isaiah 3:5 speaks of the young against the old and neighbor against neighbor; the link to divided families in Matthew 10 is the video's application.
The captions spell the towns 'Corazine,' 'Bethida' and 'Ty,' write 'crestos' for chrēstos, and 'Isaiah 3:es 1-11' for Isaiah 3:1-11.

QUESTIONS: What 'miracles' has God already shown you? How are they an invitation to repent?
Why would it be more tolerable for Sodom than for Capernaum? What does that say about the light you have received?
Where are you tempted to trust your own conclusions more than God's word?
What does it look like to stay dependent on God like a little child this week?
Read Jeremiah 6:16. What is the 'good way' you need to walk in right now?
Which burdens are you carrying that Jesus never put on you?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson for the original audience: God hides His activity from those who do not trust Him, and He reveals His activity to those who remain dependent on Him. People rejected Jesus, even in the face of His miracles, because they trusted their own conclusions about what the Messiah would do and their own understanding of what God's word teaches, and that blinded them to what God was doing in front of them. Let it sink in: this is where spiritual discernment begins. The answer to rebellion and disobedience is humility: to come to Jesus like little children, dependent and eager to be taught, and to take His yoke, which is kind and light.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): this week, before reading Scripture, pray Matthew 11:25 back to God and ask to be taught like a child. Then list one conclusion you have held tightly about God's ways, and test it against what He says.

   Daniel (Daniel 7:14, LSB): "And to Him was given dominion, / Glory, and a kingdom, / That all the peoples, nations, and men of every tongue / Might serve Him. / His dominion is an everlasting dominion / Which will not be taken away; / And His kingdom is one / Which will not be destroyed."
   Jesus (Matthew 28:18, LSB): "And Jesus came up and spoke to them, saying, “All authority has been given to Me in heaven and on earth."
   (video) 'All things have been handed over to Me by My Father' (11:27) recalls the one like a Son of Man who comes to the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7, and foreshadows the Great Commission in Matthew 28:18.
   (video) Jesus also announces His special relationship with the Father: only the Son knows the Father, and those to whom the Son wills to reveal Him.
3. The lesson: Hidden from those who do not trust
   (video) The issue was rebellion and disobedience, so the cure is humility. God hides His activity from those who do not trust Him, and He reveals it to those who remain dependent on Him.
   (video) This is where spiritual discernment begins: trusting God instead of our own conclusions.
   [Background] Paul: 'God has chosen the foolish things of the world to shame the wise' (1 Corinthians 1:27). (1 Corinthians 1:26-29)

## Take My yoke
1. Matthew 11:28-30: Come to Me
   Rest Matthew 11:28-30: "“Come to Me, all who are weary and heavy-laden, and I will give you rest. Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For My yoke is easy and My burden is light.”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+11:28-30
   (video) A yoke, the video says, is a Hebrew idiom for a rabbi's teaching. A disciple wanted to be like his rabbi in every way, and that meant total obedience and dedication to his teaching and way of life.
   [Background] Contrast the leaders who 'tie up heavy burdens and lay them on men's shoulders' (23:4). (Matthew 23:4)
2. Jeremiah 6:16: Rest for your souls
   Good way Jeremiah 6:16: "Thus says Yahweh, / “Stand by the ways and see and ask for the ancient paths, / Where the good way is, and walk in it; / And you will find rest for your souls. / But they said, ‘We will not walk in it.’" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Jeremiah+6:16
   (video) Jesus' rest is tied to Jeremiah 6:16: rest comes from walking the good path, living by the right teaching. That is why He speaks of His yoke.
   [Background] Jeremiah's hearers answered, 'We will not walk in it.' The towns of 11:20-24 answered the same way.
3. Matthew 11:30: An easy yoke
   (video) 'Easy' is chrēstos: kind, pleasant, not harsh or stern or severe. The captions spell it 'crestos.' Jesus' teaching is not a crushing load.
   [Background] 'Gentle' in 11:29 is praus, the same word as 'lowly' in the Beatitudes (5:5). (Matthew 5:5)
   [Background] A later rabbinic saying speaks of 'the yoke of the Torah' (Mishnah Avot 3:5).

## Key people
- Jesus: Grieves over the towns that would not repent, praises the Father, and offers His easy yoke. [Background] Matthew uses 'woe' again in Jesus' seven woes to the scribes and Pharisees (chapter 23).
- Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum: The towns that saw most of His miracles and did not repent. [Background] Bethsaida was the home town of Philip, Andrew and Peter (John 1:44).
- Tyre and Sidon: Gentile cities, old enemies of Israel, that would have repented. [Background] The prophets pronounced judgment on them (Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26-28).
- Sodom: The picture of pagan wickedness; still, it would have remained. [Background] Destroyed with fire from heaven (Genesis 19:24-25).
- The wise and intelligent: Those who trusted their own understanding and missed what God was doing. [Background] Compare Isaiah 29:14: 'the wisdom of their wise men will perish.'
- Infants: Humble, dependent, and eager to be taught. [Background] Nēpios: a small child; Paul uses it for immature believers (1 Corinthians 3:1).

## Places [Background]
- Capernaum (named in the video): Jesus' home base: 'will you be exalted to heaven? You will descend to Hades' (11:23).
- Chorazin (named in the video): Woe to you, Chorazin (11:21); about 3 km north of Capernaum.
- Bethsaida (named in the video): Woe to you, Bethsaida (11:21); home of Philip, Andrew and Peter (John 1:44).
- Tyre (named in the video): A Phoenician port that, Jesus says, would have repented in sackcloth and ashes (11:21).

## Key terms
- Woe: Greek ouai, a cry of grief or warning; the video prefers 'alas.'
- Sackcloth and ashes: Rough goat-hair cloth and ashes, the signs of mourning and repentance (Jonah 3:5-6). [Background]
- Hades: The realm of the dead (Hebrew Sheol); here the opposite of being 'exalted to heaven.' [Background]
- Day of judgment: The final judgment, when it will be 'more tolerable' for some than for others.
- Degrees of punishment: The idea that judgment is weighed by the light received (11:22-24; John 19:11; Luke 12:47-48).
- Eschatological: Having to do with the last things and the coming judgment; the captions spell it 'esqueological.'
- Yoke: A wooden bar that joins animals for work; in the video, an idiom for a rabbi's teaching and way of life.
- Son of Man: Jesus' favorite title for Himself, drawn from Daniel 7:13-14.

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Three towns by the lake: Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum sit within a few miles of each other on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee, where Jesus did most of His work. Today they are ruins; Chorazin's black basalt synagogue dates from centuries later.
- Tyre and Sidon: Phoenician port cities on the coast north-west of Galilee. The prophets pronounced judgment on their pride and wealth (Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26-28); Jesus later visited their region (15:21).
- Sackcloth and ashes: Mourners and penitents wore rough goat-hair cloth and sat in or sprinkled themselves with ashes, as Nineveh did when Jonah preached (Jonah 3:5-6).
- The yoke of the Torah: Later rabbinic sayings use the same picture: 'whoever takes upon himself the yoke of the Torah, they remove from him the yoke of government and the yoke of worldly concerns' (Mishnah Avot 3:5). Reciting the Shema is to 'accept upon himself the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven' (Mishnah Berakhot 2:2). The Mishnah was compiled about AD 200.

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "And not even at this does He stay His speech, but makes their fears yet more intense… so as by every means to gather them in, both by bewailing, and by alarming them." Homilies on Matthew 37, on 11:21-24. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "Wherefore neither did He say, you have revealed it to fools, but to babes; to unsophisticated, that is, to simple-minded men" Homilies on Matthew 38, on 11:25. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "Thus He both spoke of a yoke, and called it easy; both named a burden, and added that it was light; that you should neither flee from them as toilsome, nor despise them as over easy." Homilies on Matthew 38, on 11:30. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Degrees of punishment? The video takes 'more tolerable' at face value: judgment is weighed by the light received. Most commentators agree (compare Luke 12:47-48); others read the comparison as rhetorical emphasis on Israel's guilt.
- Sovereignty and responsibility The Father hides and reveals (11:25-27), yet the towns are blamed for not repenting (11:20). The video lets both stand, as Scripture does; traditions differ on how to explain them together.
- What is the yoke? The video: a rabbi's teaching. Others see a wider picture of submission, as in the 'yoke' of a king or of wisdom (compare Sirach 51:26). Either way, Jesus offers Himself, not a heavier law.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The quotes attributed to Leon Morris ('regret, which combines warning and compassion') and D. A. Carson ('dependent and… love to be taught') are summaries we could not check against the books.
- Tyre and Sidon were not always enemies: Hiram of Tyre helped David and Solomon build (1 Kings 5:1-12). The prophets' oracles against them (Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26-28) are what the video has in mind.
- 'Yoke' as an idiom for a rabbi's teaching rests mostly on later rabbinic sayings ('the yoke of the Torah,' Mishnah Avot 3:5, compiled about AD 200); it is a fair background, not a first-century definition.
- Isaiah 3:5 speaks of the young against the old and neighbor against neighbor; the link to divided families in Matthew 10 is the video's application.
- The captions spell the towns 'Corazine,' 'Bethida' and 'Ty,' write 'crestos' for chrēstos, and 'Isaiah 3:es 1-11' for Isaiah 3:1-11.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. What 'miracles' has God already shown you? How are they an invitation to repent?
2. Why would it be more tolerable for Sodom than for Capernaum? What does that say about the light you have received?
3. Where are you tempted to trust your own conclusions more than God's word?
4. What does it look like to stay dependent on God like a little child this week?
5. Read Jeremiah 6:16. What is the 'good way' you need to walk in right now?
6. Which burdens are you carrying that Jesus never put on you?

## Application
- (video) The lesson for the original audience: God hides His activity from those who do not trust Him, and He reveals His activity to those who remain dependent on Him. People rejected Jesus, even in the face of His miracles, because they trusted their own conclusions about what the Messiah would do and their own understanding of what God's word teaches, and that blinded them to what God was doing in front of them. Let it sink in: this is where spiritual discernment begins. The answer to rebellion and disobedience is humility: to come to Jesus like little children, dependent and eager to be taught, and to take His yoke, which is kind and light.
- Study note (added): this week, before reading Scripture, pray Matthew 11:25 back to God and ask to be taught like a child. Then list one conclusion you have held tightly about God's ways, and test it against what He says.
